overview: The CC Community Development Board is responsible for urban planning, zoning reform, and site plan reviews in Medford. Its work from late 2023 through 2026 has been defined by a comprehensive citywide zoning overhaul intended to align local ordinances with the city's comprehensive plan. The board evaluates special permits for commercial and residential developments, manages Community Development Block Grant performance, and develops district-specific zoning for key corridors and squares. At the most recent meeting in October 2026, the board focused on site plan modifications and draft amendments to clean up citywide zoning formatting and height definitions.

threads.name: Citywide Zoning Overhaul
threads.summary: In late 2023, the board selected consultants for an 18-month project to recodify the city's zoning ordinances. Initial efforts focused on updating use definitions, consolidating parking tables, and establishing municipal site plan review standards. By mid-2026, the board shifted toward administrative cleanup of the zoning code, addressing formatting and standardizing development incentives across all districts.

threads.name: Corridor-Specific Rezoning
threads.summary: The board has systematically developed new zoning for major transit and commercial corridors. This began with the Wellington Station Multifamily Overlay to comply with the MBTA Communities Act, followed by the Mystic Avenue Corridor District and the Salem Street Corridor. Most recently, the board spent several months in joint sessions with the City Council to refine sub-districts and student housing standards for the Boston Avenue corridor.

threads.name: Tufts University Development and Institutional Zoning
threads.summary: The board manages the unique challenges of the Tufts campus through both project-specific reviews and the creation of a dedicated institutional zone. Under the Dover Amendment, the board approved a 10-story, 677-bed dormitory and a new aquatic center, though it applied conditions related to community transparency and shuttle usage. Current efforts include drafting a Tufts Institutional Zone to regulate building heights and setbacks that were previously subject to broader commercial standards.

threads.name: Residential Zoning and ADU Reform
threads.summary: Extensive public hearings were held to establish new Neighborhood Residential and Urban Residential districts to replace existing residential codes. This work includes bringing local regulations for Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) into compliance with new state laws, which limit local authority to restrict units near transit. The board has balanced calls for increased density to mitigate the housing crisis against neighborhood concerns regarding infrastructure capacity and emergency service access.

threads.name: Medford Square and West Medford Square Rezoning
threads.summary: Zoning updates for the city's squares have focused on encouraging mixed-use density while protecting historic assets. Joint sessions with the City Council addressed building height transitions, parking flexibility, and incentives for public amenities like community solar. A major component includes the Transom project, a proposed redevelopment of the City Hall parking lot into 300 residential units and an urban grocery store.

threads.name: Affordable Housing and Development Incentives
threads.summary: The board oversees large affordable developments such as the 238-unit Walkling Court project and manages inclusionary zoning rules. In 2026, the board recommended amendments to allow fractional cash payments to the Affordable Housing Trust for small-scale developments. Recent working sessions have aimed to close loopholes in the city's incentive framework to ensure public benefits, such as pocket parks, are proportional to development bonuses.

threads.name: Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Oversight
threads.summary: The board holds annual public hearings to review the Consolidated Annual Performance and Evaluation Report (CAPER). These reviews track expenditures on infrastructure, housing rehabilitation loans, and public services funded by federal grants. Recent reports highlighted over $1 million in spending for sidewalk installations, vacant storefront grants, and playground designs.
